newsitem.title: KENYA: Kenyan business urges return to IMF fold.
newsitem.headline: Kenyan business urges return to IMF fold.

text.p: Kenyan business leaders have urged the government to take swift action to halt corruption after the International Monetary Fund (IMF) halted a multi-million dollar aid package.
The tough IMF decision rocked the East African nation and Kenyans waited for comment from President Daniel arap Moi, 73, the ruler since 1978.
Finance Minister Musalia Mudavadi said the government had expected $215 million from the IMF and other donors in this financial year before the IMF halted crucial aid on Thursday in a row over graft.
Kenya's Association of Manufacturers said in a joint statement with the Chamber of Commerce and Industry: "The IMF decision to halt aid to Kenya is very unfortunate.
"It is bad news but all is not lost. We can solve our our problems internally and we must do so," the two agencies said.
"On behalf of the business community, we request the government to do all that is necessary to stamp out corruption," they said, adding that economic reform was a must.
"We must strive to remove corruption but at the same time we need to reduce dependence on aid and aid-funded projects."

Corporate executive Chris Kirubi, who also signed the statement, told Reuters that business wanted the government to urgently return to the negotiating table with the IMF in a move that would bolster flagging investor confidence.
The business groups said they had fully taken into account consequences of the IMf decision and "there is no cause for panic by the local business fraternity".

They added that capital flight from Kenya in the light of the IMF ruling was mainly "hot money" from investments in short-term government securities. They said long-term investors had seen such volatility before and understood Kenya's environment.
"We urge all investors not to panic. Let us all do our bit...to ensure that sense prevails," they added.
Kenyan Attorney-General Amos Wako on published on Friday a tough anti-corruption bill to be debated and approved by parliament.

Under "The Statute Law (Repeals and Miscellaneous Act) Bill 1997", Wako also proposed to repeal the Vagrancy Act under which police can detain anyone on suspicion of being a vagabond and to amend various laws ranging from banking to public security.
The IMF turned down a request from Kenya for more time to try to take measures to meet IMF concerns about corruption and its demands for reform of the energy sector.
Central Bank Governor Micah Cheserem called for urgent damage limitation and said the IMF had dealt a serious blow to Kenya's international credibility.
"This is an unfortunate development but we must face it. We must not condemn (the IMF). What is important is damage limitation that will ensure the economy is not severely hurt," he told Reuters.
Some 46 percent of Kenya's 29 million population live below the poverty line and unemployment is Kenya's worst problem.
Mudavadi spoke of possible negotiations with the IMF over a shadow Enhanced Structural Adjustment Facility (ESAF) that did not involve IMF cash but would require Kenya to meet certain targets.

Kenya's opposition hailed the IMF decision, acknowledging that it would hit projects and investment but saying damage was necessary to press the government into reforms before a general election this year.

"I'm very pleased the IMF has finally recognised the enormous problem of governance in this country," said Richard Leakey, secretary-general of the unregistered Safina party which campaigned for political reforms and against corruption.
